claims.text: A multiscale simulation integrating DFT electron-phonon interactions with advanced anharmonic phonon-scattering methods will accurately and separately predict lattice and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed approach will outperform methods based on Debye-temperature estimates and analytical approximations.
The target material is a defect-minimized, single-phase, crystalline, homogeneous HfNbTaTiZr alloy comparable to experimentally characterized low-oxygen specimens.

Coupling DFT-derived electronic structures and force constants to Boltzmann transport with electron-phonon and anharmonic phonon scattering can explicitly decouple electronic and lattice thermal conductivity.
The model is applicable from approximately 300 to 1200 K for HfNbTaTiZr containing no more than 1 wt.% oxygen.
Low-temperature validation near 200 K is relevant because lattice and electronic thermal-transport contributions are comparable there.
Homogeneous mixing and short-range atomic order mediate the interplay between electronic structure and lattice dynamics in this refractory high-entropy alloy.
The advanced simulation captures the interplay between electronic structure and lattice dynamics more faithfully than earlier approaches.
Explicitly calculated phonon-scattering rates, including anharmonic interactions, determine the modeled lattice thermal conductivity.
DFT band structures and electron-phonon coupling integrated into a Boltzmann transport equation determine the modeled electronic thermal conductivity.
Debye-based estimates conflate lattice and electronic heat-transport channels.
The model will reduce prediction error from approximately 50% to 25% or less relative to experiment.
The expected accuracy improvement will be greatest in the mid-to-high temperature range.
Earlier analytical and DFT-informed approaches required a Debye temperature, generally assumed perfect defect-free crystals, and could not capture the full atomic-scale complexity.
Earlier approaches typically conflate lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions.
The predicted improvement may not hold below 200 K or in specimens containing more than approximately 1 wt.% oxygen or substantial defects.
Electron-phonon scattering rates, anharmonic effects, broad temperature ranges, and slight composition variations are significant sources of predictive uncertainty.
Laser-flash analysis, time-domain thermoreflectance, Hall measurements, and Raman spectroscopy can independently resolve the required lattice and electronic transport quantities and scattering rates.
A deviation greater than approximately 25% between separately measured and predicted lattice or electronic thermal conductivity across the specified range would falsify the hypothesis.
